presentingComplaint: Vague generalised weakness and two unwitnessed falls over 3 days, with a near-collapse this morning
history: 78-year-old woman brought by daughter with several days of progressive fatigue, heavy legs and difficulty rising from a chair; no chest pain, palpitations volunteered, or overt symptoms until a transient loss of consciousness while walking to the bathroom. Background of hypertension, type 2 diabetes and stage 3b CKD (baseline creatinine 1.6 mg/dL). Long-standing ramipril and spironolactone; primary care added trimethoprim 5 days ago for dysuria, and she has been taking ibuprofen for knee pain. Reduced oral intake for 2 days. No diarrhoea. This is deliberately an atypical, subtle presentation — no dramatic arrhythmic collapse or classic muscle cramps — dominated instead by nonspecific weakness and falls in a frail, polypharmacy patient (ACE-inhibitor + potassium-sparing diuretic + trimethoprim + NSAID 'quadruple whammy').
examination: Frail, alert but flat affect. Symmetrical proximal>distal limb weakness with globally diminished/absent deep tendon reflexes; sensation intact. No focal cranial or long-tract signs. Mildly dry mucous membranes, JVP not raised, chest clear, abdomen soft and non-tender, bladder not palpable. Peripheries warm.
imaging: Bedside ultrasound: no hydronephrosis, non-distended bladder (excludes obstructive AKI).
microbiology: Urine dipstick trace leucocytes, nitrite negative; not clinically infected. Blood cultures not indicated.
differentialDiagnoses: Severe hyperkalaemia with hyperkalaemic muscle weakness and bradyarrhythmia (drug-induced, on background of AKI-on-CKD)
Acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease
Primary neuromuscular cause of falls (excluded by reflex pattern and biochemistry)
finalDiagnosis: Severe hyperkalaemia (K+ 7.3 mmol/L) presenting atypically as weakness, falls and bradycardia — precipitated by RAAS blockade + spironolactone + trimethoprim + NSAID on AKI-on-CKD
citations: UK Kidney Association — Treatment of Acute Hyperkalaemia in Adults, 2023
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Fluid and Electrolyte Disturbances (Potassium), 2022
stewardship: Not applicable — non-infective metabolic emergency. Discontinue offending agents (ramipril, spironolactone, trimethoprim, ibuprofen).
contraindications: Avoid IV calcium in the same line as bicarbonate (precipitation)
Do not give insulin-dextrose without capillary glucose monitoring for delayed hypoglycaemia
Avoid further potassium-sparing/RAAS agents and NSAIDs
Caution with salbutamol as sole agent; it is adjunctive, not definitive
edgeCases: ECG may look deceptively benign or show only bradycardia/absent P waves rather than classic peaked T waves — do not be reassured
Hyperkalaemic paralysis can mimic Guillain-Barré (ascending weakness, areflexia) but resolves rapidly with potassium correction
Trimethoprim blocks the distal nephron ENaC channel like amiloride, a commonly missed precipitant
Refractory hyperkalaemia with oligoanuric AKI may need emergency haemodialysis
expectedMaiK: Recognise severe hyperkalaemia as the unifying cause of weakness, areflexia and bradycardia in a frail patient on multiple potassium-retaining drugs; obtain immediate ECG and give IV calcium for myocardial protection, then insulin-dextrose ± salbutamol to shift potassium, address AKI and stop all offending agents.
expectedNextQuestions: Full medication and over-the-counter/NSAID history and any recent new prescriptions?
Urine output over the last 24-48 hours and fluid intake?
Any potassium-rich salt substitutes or supplements?
Prior baseline renal function and potassium values?
expectedInvestigations: Urea, electrolytes and creatinine (compare to baseline)
regressionAssertions: Management must include IV calcium for myocardial membrane stabilisation
Management must include a potassium-shifting agent (insulin-dextrose)
Must advise stopping the precipitant drugs (ACE-inhibitor, spironolactone, trimethoprim, NSAID)
Must not label this as primarily infective / must set stewardship tier to null
